note: Several sites' opportunity screens combined: where each question fired and the data to collect at each. A screen, not an audit: no savings are computed and nothing is ranked by value; the order is only how many sites a question fired at, then how many findings.

questions.question: What do existing records establish about this utility user's measurement coverage, usable data and intended decision?

data_requests.item: Utility flow to this user
data_requests.how: A same-stream, same-user/medium or nearby flow candidate may be useful evidence but does not automatically settle exact coverage, quantity, comparability or usable data. Another branch, foreign/unavailable or old/FAULT source, an unqualified totalizer and a site bill cannot establish this user's representative consumption. S22 distinguishes measurement approaches and their limitations; review fit-for-purpose existing records first, including suitable compensated steam data and fluid-dependent technology/installation constraints. No compulsory clamp-on/spool, production interruption or allocation from site totals is authorized.

where: site records: Existing exact utility/branch/user and meter/tag/source associations; quantity and units, actual versus reference volume/mass/energy/rate/total basis and necessary compensation, sample interval/time/coverage and production basis; availability/access, quality/gaps, calibration/range/installation/maintenance and source/revision records.

a walkdown: Only if an applicable question remains after reviewing existing records, agree safe additional observations with the responsible engineer; no mandatory new meter, field test, operating change or equipment replacement.

data_requests.item: Who would use the reading
data_requests.how: S22 printed3.1-3.14 and4.1-4.5 distinguishes purpose and analysis/action from merely having a meter and requires ongoing quality/maintenance/data-loss review. Match resolution, coverage and usable records to the decision. Existing suitable data/report use can be acknowledged without another meter; an unread meter, arbitrary proximity or billing total alone does not establish a saving or meaningful end-use allocation. The guide's building examples and S19 historical monitoring table are not this process's measured benefit, design authority or compliance finding.

where: site records: Existing energy/production report or decision, intended data user and review responsibilities, required resolution/time and performance, lifecycle/installation/analysis resources and constraints; identify unresolved source/coverage and review any proposed additional measurement.

questions.decision_rule: Review exact utility/user/branch and measurement/source associations, usable quantity/time/quality/coverage and the intended decision/report with the responsible specialist. Retain candidates and unknowns without inferring installed absence or completed data collection from a nearby flow tag. Acknowledge suitable existing measurement or nonapplicability before proposing further work; any new metering requires a purpose-specific technology, installation/lifecycle and access review. No automatic instrument installation, allocation or site savings follows.

typical_benefit.wording: "You can't manage what do don't measure" [sic]. Buildings: "efficiency improvements of 10-20%." The guide warns "only success stories are published" and that savings come only if action is taken. LBNL Monitoring & Targeting (as reported in LBNL-56183): "Typical savings 4-17%, average 8%" (UK experience).
source_titles: S22: FEMP Metering Best Practices: A Guide to Achieving Utility Resource Efficiency, Release 3.0 (PNNL-23892, Mar 2015)
S19: Worrell & Galitsky, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for Petroleum Refineries: An ENERGY STAR Guide (LBNL-56183, Feb 2005)

questions.question: What do existing records establish about these measurements' purpose, readers and remaining source/logic coverage?

data_requests.item: Whether operators adjust anything by hand from these readings
data_requests.how: Frequent manual adjustment can justify a control investigation, not automatic automation. A reading with no routine manual action may have a legitimate abnormal/alarm/protection/indication purpose; do not close it solely because nobody regularly acts. Acknowledge suitable existing purpose, manual or automatic operation, and record unresolved function/source suitability. No operator trial, live change or benefit is inferred.

where: site records: Existing exact measurement/source identity and quantity, actual indication/control/alarm/protection/recording purpose, normal and abnormal decisions, operator logs/round sheets and current availability/quality/coverage; retain per-subject association and source/revision.

data_requests.item: The control system's own loop list
data_requests.how: A controller or interlock reference is useful supplied evidence, not proof of complete current logic, correct process meaning, safety adequacy or measurement authority. A partial model without controllers can still prompt existing-record clarification; it does not prove no installed controls or require a fabricated loop list. S19 printed30 is broad monitoring/process-control guidance, not a per-reading automation acceptance test.

where: site records: Existing current loop/point list, cause/effect, alarm/sequence/configuration and represented reader/interlock/source records; preserve exact endpoints and identify missing model coverage before concluding indication-only.

questions.decision_rule: Review measurement purpose and actual normal/abnormal decisions, represented readers and source/logic coverage with the responsible specialist. Neither a missing model controller nor a represented reader settles installed control completeness or the need for automation. Suitable existing use or nonapplicability can be acknowledged; unresolved records remain explicit. No automatic upgrade, safety acceptance or source-reported saving is assigned.

questions.question: What valve-position feedback and diagnostic records are available for these control valves?

data_requests.item: Existing valve/loop feedback and diagnostic records
data_requests.how: For each named valve/loop, review the record target, revision/locator, declared signal function, units, enabled return path and diagnostic capability. Keep command/current/travel setpoint separate from measured stem or shaft travel; local positioner feedback does not establish control-room or historian availability. Nearby Z tags and shared unit/stream membership do not establish valve association. Acknowledge appropriate existing coverage, including endpoint indication for an on/off duty, and retain unresolved source questions. Supplied fields do not complete this review.

where: DCS/PLC configuration: approved existing valve/positioner configuration and point definitions for each named valve and loop
maintenance records: existing valve, positioner and calibration records
site records: approved loop drawings, I/O mappings, source revisions and locators

data_requests.item: Existing valve performance and diagnostic history
data_requests.how: Review available history first. Retain valve/loop identity, source revision/locator, time and operating conditions, enabled state, quality/calibration and readability. Where suitable, compare command, independently described travel and process response over coincident periods. Position indication, endpoint states or oscillation alone do not diagnose stiction or its cause. Keep disabled, bad-quality, unavailable, foreign and unknown records as qualified candidates; ask the responsible record owner for the missing basis. This screen specifies no new manual step test, loop-mode change or operating experiment.

questions.decision_rule: Record appropriate existing feedback/diagnostics as coverage with its source scope and remaining gaps. Route a named valve/loop request to the responsible record owner where function, association, availability or performance evidence is unresolved. Configuration, tuning, process and assembly causes remain open when investigating reported behavior. Any further test or change requires a separate company-approved method and operating/outage decision; this finding prescribes no retrofit, retune, new connection or mode change.

typical_benefit.wording: S13 discusses backlash/stiction and variability in highly throttled/oversized pumping systems, not a universal feedback retrofit. S29-S32 distinguish feedback routes and vendor-specific diagnostic/history examples. They establish no quantified benefit for this investigation or the supplied plant.

questions.question: What source-labelled trip or interlock records apply to each rotating or fired machine, and what remains unverified?

data_requests.item: Cause-and-effect matrix and HAZOP/LOPA records
data_requests.how: Review existing cause-and-effect, governing requirements and configuration records for each named machine, with their revisions and applicability. Retain supplied trip/switch indications as candidates; a drawing label or an unrelated function does not settle the records or establish effective, tested protection. Missing model information is not evidence that installed protection is absent.

where: site records: cause-and-effect matrix, HAZOP and LOPA reports
DCS/PLC configuration: safety system configuration
site records: cause-and-effect matrix, HAZOP and LOPA reports

data_requests.item: Machine/function association and current evidence
data_requests.how: Keep each machine in the review even where a switch or trip is supplied. Retain all explicit shared targets and supplied qualifiers; unknown or contradictory targets remain unresolved. Same-model text or nearby equipment does not prove function coverage. Record a responsible person or authority separately from protected-machine association; neither is inferred here. This requests record review, not a new test, safety design or operating action.

where: site records: source-labelled function identifiers, initiating measurements, final elements and protected-machine targets, shared scope and revisions; governing requirements and validation/test evidence where applicable

questions.decision_rule: A qualified site review may resolve the source-labelled machine/function associations and remaining record requests using applicable current evidence. A supplied trip, switch, cause/effect row or shared-function label alone establishes neither complete coverage nor installed protection adequacy. This screen grants no acceptance or authority and performs no safety validation.

typical_benefit.wording: Safety benefit; no energy source. Present it as a question to verify, not a finding.

questions.question: What records support this refrigeration compressor's part-load control, sequencing and real-input basis?

data_requests.item: Capacity-control mode and representative load for this compressor
data_requests.how: Retain labels and enabled/disabled/unknown qualifiers as candidates. Establish actual function and a representative operating basis; a nameplate or drive label does not establish part-load behavior.

where: DCS/PLC configuration: existing identified compressor configuration and active/fallback mode, slide-valve or bypass function, revision and responsible owner
site records: permitted load/capacity histories with machine identity, period and coincident suction/demand conditions

data_requests.item: Representative real input power on the same operating basis
data_requests.how: Compare suitable coincident input and load records. Separate ratings, electrical indications and near-full-load conditions from actual representative real input; request missing evidence without inventing a value or authorizing measurements.

where: site records: approved existing electrical-input and run/load observations with quantity, units, time and conversion basis
the vendor datasheet: applicable compressor/drive limits and part-load performance basis
historian or DCS trend for JT-201 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)

data_requests.item: Actual sequencing, served group and applicable supplier constraints
data_requests.how: A sequencer label alone does not establish active operation or complete group coverage. Return a qualified partial answer or missing-evidence request to the responsible reviewer.

where: DCS/PLC configuration: existing reviewed sequence/trim logic, machine-to-suction-group association, active overrides and revision
site records: permitted operating/event records showing which machines actually trim under comparable conditions
the vendor datasheet: applicable supplier constraints and responsible engineering review route

questions.decision_rule: Investigate missing or conflicting source/function/operating evidence for each named machine. A drive or sequencing label does not settle efficiency, and the source describes load-dependent tradeoffs. Close only the source investigation after qualified evidence review; no drive change, operating instruction or savings estimate follows.

typical_benefit.wording: Among control strategies that "may compromise system energy efficiency" (S25, p. 59, citing Pearson 2003): "Slide valve unloading of oversized screw compressors." and "Hot gas bypass of compressors." Speed control (S25, p. 63): "ASDs used on compressors below a part-load ratio of about 95% will deliver performance equal to a fixed speed compressor but with lower electricity requirements. However, at near full (i.e., 100%) load, ASDs are approximately 3% less efficient than fixed speed drives".
source_titles: S25: Brush, Masanet and Worrell, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Dairy Processing Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers (LBNL-6261E, Oct 2011)

data_requests.how: S26 describes indirect circulating-medium/run-around recovery as an option when local duct space is limited; assess applicability rather than treating lack of nearby direct-duct space as universal closure. questions.decision_rule: Use qualified existing records to distinguish working full coverage, unavailable or partial recovery and unresolved own-inlet/process-use questions. A responsible engineer can answer or defer the investigation from an adequate documented basis; no new project is compulsory. Missing local duct space or intermittent operation alone is not an automatic universal closure.

typical_benefit.wording: Dryers (S26, p. 104): "A simple form of heat recovery in retrofit applications is to utilize the exhaust air of a dryer to preheat the inlet air stream, thereby saving energy." Spray dryers (S25, p. 90): "It is estimated that up to 30% of the heat from the dryer exhaust can be recovered." Fryers (S26, p. 107): "Conditioning of the exhaust gas is required, however, to remove fats and to reduce fouling of the heat exchange system." No source in this set gives a figure for ovens.

questions.question: What do existing records establish about this represented burner air-fuel operating basis, the supplied analysis or metering candidates and applicable process-air constraints?

data_requests.item: Existing air-fuel or flue-analysis, tuning and calibration records
data_requests.how: Use an appropriate flow-metering, flue-analysis or combined method; a permanently installed O2 analyser is not mandatory. An oxygen/composition label may refer to product or another purpose and is not a flue-combustion basis. Preserve supplied false, zero and unknown values without qualifying them as actual function, calibration or performance.

where: site records: approved existing burner tuning, paired air/fuel flow-metering or flue-analysis reports, or their combination, with equipment, author/owner, date, quantity, sampling location, units/basis and high/low-fire or representative load coverage
maintenance records: existing analyser/meter calibration, maintenance and suitability records and the reported flue oxygen/combustibles and exhaust-temperature context where available

data_requests.item: Existing ratio-control function and applicable equipment guidance
data_requests.how: Separate a named ratio, analyser or enabled flag from reviewed as-operated evidence. Compare only on an applicable documented fuel, operating and method basis; this screen supplies no universal O2 target, ratio setting or adjustment permission.

where: site records: approved existing burner/ratio-control configuration, active/fallback or manual mode, linkage or trim basis, revision and identified responsible owner
the vendor datasheet: applicable burner/equipment guidance and documented air-fuel/excess-air requirements across its operating range
DCS/PLC configuration: permitted existing burner-management and ratio-control configuration records, only through the company-approved access route

data_requests.item: Existing fuel and production records for an appropriate operating basis
data_requests.how: Keep high/low-fire or other representative load evidence distinct from a nominal rating or an isolated number. No fixed month, new logging task, efficiency result or fuel-saving estimate is inferred.

where: site records: approved existing identified fuel/input and production/load records over a justified representative period, including dates, units and relevant conditions
utility bills or the site energy report: existing identified unit fuel sub-meter records where suitable for the proposed comparison

questions.decision_rule: Use qualified existing records to establish the applicable combustion and process-air basis and identify unresolved method, calibration, load or constraint evidence. Either appropriate air/fuel metering, flue analysis or a combination can support the review. Neither presence nor absence of a label establishes efficiency, a fault or need for adjustment. A responsible company reviewer can answer from adequate records or define a separately approved follow-up; this screen does not select operating settings.

typical_benefit.wording: S27 (p. 1): "Periodic checking and resetting of air-fuel ratios for burners is one of the simplest ways to get maximum efficiency out of fuel-fired process heating equipment such as furnaces, ovens, heaters, and boilers." And: "Processes that evaporate moisture or solvents need large amounts of excess air to dilute flammable solvents to noncombustible levels, to ensure adequate drying rates, and to carry vapors out of the oven. Lowering excess air to minimal levels can slow down the process and create an explosion hazard." No typical % stated (the sheet's worked example is one furnace).
source_titles: S27: DOE Industrial Technologies Program, Process Heating Tip Sheet #2, Check Burner Air to Fuel Ratios (Nov 2007)

Distinguish documented working full coverage from unresolved partial, disabled, shared or internal-only recovery. A qualified company review can answer or defer the question from existing records; unknown evidence is not an automatic otherwise-close result, a feasible project or a mandate for a new project.

typical_benefit.wording: S28 (p. 1): "many companies install heat exchangers on the exhaust stacks of furnaces and ovens to produce hot water or to generate hot air for space heating." The same sheet: "The temperature difference between the primary and secondary process should be high enough (at least 200°F), and there should be a sufficient amount of usable waste heat." Fryers (S26, p. 107): "Heat can be recovered indirectly from a fryer's fat-laden exhaust gases via a heat exchange system and used for pre-heating air and water for use in other facility processes." No % stated.

questions.question: Is this hot line insulated?

data_requests.item: Insulation condition and length of bare pipe
data_requests.how: Retain the identified line/location, survey date/revision, condition, length and pipe-size basis. Missing insulation metadata does not establish a bare line. Record unavailable or unsuitable evidence; new observations require the receiving organization's approved process.

where: site records: approved existing line list, insulation survey and inspection records

data_requests.item: Applicable surface-temperature and insulation evidence
data_requests.how: Review line identity/location, source revision/date, surface versus fluid/design meaning, geometry and operating/ambient/time basis. Retain unreadable, wrong-asset, Boolean and unknown candidates without treating them as applicable evidence. Identify deliberate cooling or process constraints; no new live inspection, insulation installation or saving is established.

where: site records: approved existing surface/insulation records or suitable documented analysis for this line

data_requests.item: Stated line/process temperature
data_requests.how: Retain the stated temperature and original source/basis. A process-fluid or design temperature is not an actual surface-temperature measurement or a completed insulation evaluation.

where: site records: identified source temperature field and its stated basis

questions.decision_rule: Refer for engineering investigation when applicable evidence shows bare or damaged insulation on a hot line and no deliberate cooling or process constraint rules it out. The cited surface-temperature criterion is a source screening reference, not an automatic site instruction. Close only the bounded investigation when reviewed evidence settles its scope; this screen does not authorize insulation work.

typical_benefit.wording: "Insulation can typically reduce energy losses by 90%." "Any surface over 120°F should be insulated." LBNL (as reported in LBNL-56183): insulation 3-13%, 1.1 yr.

site records: The following pressure/control tag/series locations are candidate-only lookup aids from supplied records; compressor/system association, source identity, availability, measurement location and requirements remain unverified. Unknown scope or dynamic basis remains a records question, and suitable existing operation or nonapplicability may be acknowledged; no operating change or site savings are calculated.

S11 printed43-44 does not endorse a universal gallons-per-cfm rule. A known compressor package is not excluded merely because its name mentions a dryer; helpers and known nonair machines are not air subjects. Acknowledge suitable existing coverage before additional work; no obligatory one-week logging, receiver installation, compressor stop or pressure change is authorized.

where: site records: Existing actual compressor/system, critical end-use pressure and air quality, control/capacity mode, receiver volumes and location/coverage, peak magnitude/duration and interval, pressure differential, available compressor supply during events and replenishment/recovery time; source, units and comparable operating periods retained.

data_requests.how: S11 printed58-59 describes heat fractions and different air-cooled/water-cooled arrangements. Electrical input converted to heat and a recovered fraction of available thermal energy are not electrical savings or a useful site duty. Establish compatible temperatures, coincident demand and source/configuration first; the source says this heat is usually insufficient for direct steam production. Nearby load or long hours alone is insufficient. Retain required compressor cooling, ventilation/backpressure, water-quality/material and control constraints and added fan/exchanger effects. Acknowledge suitable existing recovery or nonapplicability; missing coverage remains conditional rather than a forced field test or new exchanger.

questions.question: What do existing records establish about this direct temperature-to-steam-valve control candidate's configuration, disturbances and suitable dynamics?

data_requests.item: Loop behaviour
data_requests.how: A flow-controller reference sharing the valve does not prove a nested cascade or justify suppression of conflicting/unknown configuration. The explicit additional Siemens AD353-128 rev2 April2012 pp1-4 describes a measurable/controllable secondary affecting the primary, encompassing the relevant disturbance and responding substantially faster. It also identifies disturbances outside that secondary loop and alternative secondary variables. Review the actual chain/dynamics, operating range and required behavior first; neither an oscillation nor a pressure swing alone authorizes a flow slave or tuning test. Suitable existing operation can be acknowledged.

where: site records: Existing exact measurement/controller/output and setpoint-chain/configuration, active modes, source/coverage, process objective and matched primary/secondary response, flow measurement/actuator suitability and existing load-disturbance histories.
DCS/PLC configuration: Review existing controller configuration, tuning/modes and output history; no change is requested.

a walkdown: Only if applicable questions remain after existing-record review, agree safe additional observations with the responsible specialist; no mandatory live test, sampling, shutdown, tuning, instrument or equipment change.

data_requests.item: Steam header pressure swings
data_requests.how: The manufacturer example is contextual application engineering, not a universal speed ratio, procurement or tuning requirement. Confirm that a secondary could address the relevant disturbance before any proposed design. Preserve limits and suitable transfer/reset/operating modes; a proper represented temperature-to-flow-setpoint chain is outside this direct-output pattern, not proof every cascade is adequate. No step test, setpoint/pressure change or equipment addition follows.

where: site records: Existing comparable header/valve/flow/primary-variable pressure and disturbance records, sample periods and units, control ranges/limits, transfer/tracking/reset/anti-windup and actuator/measurement constraints.

a walkdown: Only if applicable questions remain after existing-record review, agree safe additional observations with the responsible specialist; no mandatory live test, sampling, shutdown, tuning, instrument or equipment change.

Shared output labels or supply-pressure variation do not establish a cascade, its absence or a requirement to add one. Suitable existing control or nonapplicability can be acknowledged; unresolved configuration/source evidence remains a records question without tuning or operating authority.

typical_benefit.wording: No public numeric source found. Report as qualitative only.

questions.question: What do existing records establish about these relief/flare/vent candidates' actual events, measurement/composition and source coverage?

data_requests.item: Flare or vent flow and composition
data_requests.how: Same-stream flow labeling is useful candidate evidence, not complete current flow/composition/event coverage. Retain foreign, inaccessible, FAULT or unqualified totalizer data without treating it as suitable. S19 printed34-35 distinguishes planned intermittent/continuous background from upset-blowdown and describes manufacturer minimum-flow context; rare relief events or a zero lift count alone do not automatically close source/safety/environmental review. Review suitable existing records first; no generic analyzer or meter closes all quantities. Any additional measurement/recovery proposal must preserve safety paths and undergo responsible hazard/environmental review, not be imposed from a drawing clue.

where: site records: Existing exact service/path and measurement/source/event associations; quantity/rate/total/reference units, sample periods and quality/availability/gaps, composition/variability and planned intermittent/continuous versus upset/blowdown/relief records, purge/pilot/manufacturer requirements and safety/environmental basis.
site records: Review existing relief-valve lift, flare/vent and operating-event records with their actual time/source coverage.

a walkdown: Only if applicable questions remain after existing-record review, agree safe additional observations with the responsible specialist; no mandatory live test, sampling, shutdown, tuning, instrument or equipment change.

questions.decision_rule: Review exact relief/vent/flare service, planned and abnormal event coverage and usable quantity/composition/time/source records with the responsible safety/environmental and operating specialists. A flow candidate or rare-event label does not establish suitable data, completeness or safe closure. Existing appropriate records/nonapplicability can be acknowledged; unresolved evidence remains explicit. No live metering, recovery modification, reduced purge/minimum flow or operating change is authorized.

questions.question: Is this refrigeration condenser train's head pressure appropriate for its weather, operating limits and actual reset coverage?

data_requests.item: Ambient wet-bulb temperature (dry-bulb for an air-cooled condenser) at the same times
data_requests.how: Line it up hour by hour with the condensing temperature.

data_requests.how: This is the floor a floating setpoint may not go below.

where: DCS/PLC configuration: the minimum needed for hot gas defrost, liquid injection oil cooling and liquid feed to the farthest evaporator
the vendor datasheet: compressor and expansion valve minimum pressure difference

data_requests.item: Compressor and condenser fan and pump power
data_requests.how: Floating the head pressure moves load from the compressors to the condenser fans; count both.

data_requests.item: Condenser-train coverage and applicable head-pressure operating basis
data_requests.how: Keep this condenser train in the review even when local, shared, unrelated, negated or disabled reset text is supplied. Such records are candidates, not proof of current mode, complete coverage or suitable data. Verify exact train membership, pressure units/reference, refrigerant and saturation basis, appropriate wet-bulb or dry-bulb weather/sensor basis, coincident periods and relevant defrost, oil-cooling, feed and vendor constraints. Retain raw targets, revisions and qualifiers; unknown or contradictory scope stays unresolved. Compare total affected compressor and condenser fan/pump demand before drawing an economic conclusion. This requests existing records and qualified review, not a setpoint change, control design or operating action.

where: site records: source-labelled compressor discharge/header, condenser, sensor, controller, fan/pump and served-demand membership; actual reset scope, enabled/as-operated mode, revision and unknown or contradictory targets for this train

questions.decision_rule: Review only after source-qualified train membership, actual operating/reset mode, coincident representative observations, applicable pressure limits and total affected power are established. Fixed-head behavior may justify investigation, while an operating reset may narrow the question, but a supplied label or one scalar does not close coverage or suitability. No setpoint or operating change is inferred.

typical_benefit.wording: Floating head pressure (S25, p. 62) "allows compressor head pressures to move up or down with variations in ambient wet-bulb temperature, saving energy compared to fixed head pressure operation." Condensing pressure (S25, p. 65): "Lowering the condensing temperature can reduce compressor energy use by around 2% to 3% for every degree Celsius (1.8 degrees Fahrenheit) of temperature reduction (SenterNovem 2003)." Condenser fans (S25, p. 65): "On systems where floating head operation is stable, ASDs can lower condenser fan energy consumption by up to 40% compared to operating a fixed-speed condenser fan in on/off fashion (IRC 2004b)."

questions.question: Does each refrigeration suction level match the conditions required by every coincident load it serves?

data_requests.item: Suction pressure at each suction level, hourly
data_requests.how: Retain refrigerant identity, pressure reference and measurement location before relating suction pressure to saturated evaporating temperature. Match the operating periods of pressures, setpoints and loads; distinguish stages and pressure drops. No setpoint is calculated here.

where: historian or DCS trend for PT-201, PT-202 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)
DCS/PLC configuration: suction pressure setpoints per compressor or suction level

data_requests.item: The temperature each load actually needs
data_requests.how: For every coincident load, establish its required temperature and required heat-transfer approach, and the suction level actually serving it. The most demanding admissible evaporating condition across those loads constrains a shared level; the warmest load alone does not govern. This is an engineering constraint to review, not a quotation from the cited two-stage example or a plant setpoint recommendation.

where: site records: room and product temperature specifications for each freezer, cold store and chiller, and which suction level serves it
historian or DCS trend for TT-205, TT-206 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)

data_requests.item: Compressor power and run hours per suction level
data_requests.how: A month or more at normal production.

where: historian or DCS trend for JT-201 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)
site records: compressor run hours from the refrigeration plant controls

data_requests.item: Suction-level membership and reset coverage
data_requests.how: Drawn reset indications are candidates only. Confirm ownership and shared-level coverage; a reset on another compressor does not settle these loads. Unknown connections, applicable approaches and product or quality constraints remain open for qualified review.

where: site records: source-labelled compressor, suction header and served-load membership; reset strategy and coverage for each level, with stage and pressure-regulation boundaries

questions.decision_rule: Study a level only after mapping every coincident served load and reviewing its required temperature, approach and operating constraints against the actual level and reset coverage. A colder-than-required level may warrant investigation, but the most demanding admissible evaporating condition across all served loads constrains any change. A drawn reset, ambient change or warm load alone does not settle the question. The cited benefit remains a conditional two-stage low-stage example; no setpoint or savings is calculated.

typical_benefit.wording: Two-stage systems (S25, p. 63): "a simple way to save energy is to raise the suction pressure and temperature of the low-stage compressor when ambient temperatures decrease. It has been estimated that energy savings of about 8% can be realized in two-stage systems when suction temperatures are raised from -30 °F to -20 °F (ISU 2005)." No figure is given there for single-stage systems.
source_titles: S25: Brush, Masanet and Worrell, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Dairy Processing Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers (LBNL-6261E, Oct 2011)

questions.question: Is refrigeration condenser heat rejected while a low-grade heating duty nearby is met with fuel or steam?

data_requests.item: Discharge and condensing temperatures
data_requests.how: Discharge superheat is the hotter, smaller part; condensing heat is larger but only at the condensing temperature.

where: historian or DCS trend for PT-203, TT-202 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)
DCS/PLC configuration: discharge temperature and head pressure readings in the refrigeration plant controls

data_requests.item: Compressor power and run hours
data_requests.how: Heat rejected is about the compressor power plus the refrigeration load at the same time.

where: historian or DCS trend for JT-201 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)
site records: compressor run hours from the refrigeration plant controls

data_requests.item: The low-grade duty: temperature needed, load and hours
data_requests.how: Match by temperature, hours and distance.

where: site records: temperatures and loads of the hot water, CIP, wash water, floor heating and space heating users, by hour

data_requests.item: Effect on head pressure
data_requests.how: Recovery that raises the head pressure in cool weather costs compressor power (see E27); count it.

where: the vendor datasheet: whether a heat recovery exchanger would need a higher condensing pressure than now

data_requests.item: Recovery coverage by refrigeration train and heating duty
data_requests.how: A recovery device elsewhere does not establish coverage here. Retain drawn indications as candidates and verify which train and sink they serve, whether useful duty is already met, and remaining coincident heat. Keep temperatures, isolation, compressor-power/head-pressure effects and required site review explicit; no installation mandate or savings is inferred.

where: site records: source-labelled connections, heat delivered and operating periods for each existing refrigeration recovery device and served heating duty
a walkdown: confirm boundaries, distance and separation or contamination constraints for the candidate source and sink

questions.decision_rule: Worth a study when the refrigeration plant runs at the same times as a duty that needs heat below the discharge or condensing temperature, and recovery does not force the head pressure up. Close this screening investigation if the duties do not overlap or recovery would need a higher condensing pressure all year.

typical_benefit.wording: S25 (p. 64), refrigeration compressors: "Where economically feasible, rejected heat can be recovered from compressors and used in other facility applications, such as space heating or water heating." No % stated there for refrigeration (the air compressor heat recovery figures quoted under E23 do not apply).
source_titles: S25: Brush, Masanet and Worrell, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Dairy Processing Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers (LBNL-6261E, Oct 2011)

questions.question: Is representative real input power available for each refrigeration compressor, with a usable coincident load and operating basis?

data_requests.item: Compressor power
data_requests.how: Retain the original reading type, units and source claim for each named compressor; collect a representative coincident period at known production. A field labelled power or kW remains a supplied candidate and does not prove representative real input power. Amperes, volts, apparent kVA, reactive kvar and a bare cumulative kWh tag are different quantities. Appropriate voltage/current/power-factor and phase evidence, or an energy difference over an explicit matching interval, may support a documented conversion; no conversion or suitability acceptance is automated.

where: a walkdown: the drive's or motor protection relay's kW reading, or a temporary power logger, per compressor
utility bills or the site energy report: site interval meter data to apportion

data_requests.item: Suction and discharge pressures logged at the same times
data_requests.how: Logged together with power, these show how the plant runs.

where: historian or DCS trend for PT-201, PT-202 (no historian tag is mapped in this model for these)
DCS/PLC configuration: suction and discharge pressure per compressor in the refrigeration plant controls

data_requests.item: What to normalise against
data_requests.how: kW per unit of product or per unit of refrigeration.

where: site records: production throughput or freezer and cold store loads by day

data_requests.item: Applicable real-input-power and coincident operating basis
data_requests.how: Keep current, voltage, uncertain power, apparent, reactive, cumulative-energy and explicitly real-kW-labelled candidates visible. Correct attribution, quantity, time/conversion basis and representative operating conditions must be reviewed even where a real-power instrument is drawn. A supplied label or rating cannot settle actual collection or confer approval; use existing records where suitable.

where: site records: source-labelled quantity and units, circuit or compressor identity, phase and conversion basis, matching measurement interval, and data suitability review for each supplied electrical reading
DCS/PLC configuration: availability and meaning of existing actual real-power readings and synchronized operating/load records before arranging any further collection

questions.decision_rule: Review the attributed real-input quantity, matching observations, production or refrigeration load and operating conditions before deciding whether additional collection would improve a concrete decision. Existing electrical readings are candidates, including supplied real-kW claims; no tag or quantity field automatically validates the actual basis. A reading nobody reviews establishes no benefit.

typical_benefit.wording: S25 (p. 58): "A basic monitoring system should include ongoing measurement and logging of compressor suction and discharge pressures; a drop in suction pressure typically indicates a refrigerant leak, while a rise in discharge pressure can indicate a blocked condenser (EEBPP 2000a)." "In a review of energy efficiency opportunities for refrigeration systems in wineries, the energy savings associated with the installation of monitoring systems were estimated at 3% (Galitsky et al. 2005b)."
source_titles: S25: Brush, Masanet and Worrell, Energy Efficiency Improvement and Cost Saving Opportunities for the Dairy Processing Industry: An ENERGY STAR Guide for Energy and Plant Managers (LBNL-6261E, Oct 2011)
